title: Better money habits: change a habit, borrow wisely, spot scams

say: Better money habits: change a habit, borrow wisely, and spot scams.
This is the video for Module 4, Building Better Financial Habits.
Most money problems come from small habits repeated many times: a daily snack, a weekly bet, lending without writing anything down.
A habit is a loop. The cue is the trigger, like payday or a WhatsApp status.

say: To change a habit, keep the cue and the reward, but swap the routine for a better one.

say: For example, Chinwe, a civil servant in Owerri, went to the mall with friends every payday and spent about 35,000 naira.
Now, on payday morning, she moves 25,000 naira to savings first, then meets her friends for a cheaper outing with a set 8,000 naira.
Over 12 months she saves about 300,000 naira, and still enjoys time with friends. She kept the cue and the reward. That is why the change lasted.
Before borrowing, ask for three numbers in writing: how much you receive, how much you repay in total, and by when.

For example, Ruth needs about 50,000 naira for stock. A digital lender wants 62,500 back in 30 days. That costs 12,500, which is 25 percent for one month. The stock will earn her only about 10,000, so she would lose money.

panel.heading: Ruth compares two loans of 50,000 naira

say: Her registered cooperative wants 5,500 a month for 10 months, 55,000 in total. The cost is 5,000 naira, and she still gains. Ruth chooses Loan B.
Compare the total amount repaid, not just the monthly payment or the speed of approval.

say: Know these three scams. First, someone promises a loan or grant but asks for a processing, insurance or registration fee first. Do not pay.

cards.d: A loan or grant that needs a processing fee first. Genuine lenders do not ask you to pay to receive a loan.
Callers asking for your BVN, card details, PIN or OTP. Banks never ask for these.
Old members paid with new members' money. It always collapses, and most people lose.

say: Second, callers claim to be from your bank and ask for your BVN, card details, PIN or OTP. Banks never ask for these.

cards.d: A loan or grant that needs a processing fee first. Genuine lenders do not ask you to pay to receive a loan.
Callers asking for your BVN, card details, PIN or OTP. Banks never ask for these.

say: Third, ponzi schemes. They pay earlier members with money from newer members, not real profits. MMM Nigeria froze members' accounts in December 2016, and many lost their savings.
Warning signs are guaranteed high returns, pressure to act fast, rewards for recruiting, payment into a personal account, and no registration with SEC Nigeria.

say: Check loan apps on the FCCPC list, investment platforms with SEC Nigeria, and banks with the CBN. An app that wants all your contacts and photos is a warning sign.

If you have sent money to a fraudster, contact your bank immediately through its official channels and report to the police. And if betting is taking over in your home, delete the apps, tell a trusted person, and seek support.

say: Goals give your saving a direction. A SMART goal is specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound.
For example, Hauwa makes kunu and zobo in Zaria. She will save about 180,000 naira for a second cooking pot, a chest cooler and packaging by 30 June.

panel.heading: Hauwa's goal: 180,000 naira in 9 months
items: Specific: second pot, cooler and packaging
Into a locked target savings plan
Balance on a wall chart each month

say: 180,000 divided by 9 months is about 20,000 a month, or about 5,000 a week.

say: Children learn money habits mostly by watching adults. For example, Ifeoma gives her son Chidi about 1,000 naira a week for sweeping and washing plates.
They agree on three jars: 500 naira to Save, 300 to Spend, and 200 to Share.
Chidi wants a football costing about 5,000 naira. With 500 a week, he gets there in 10 weeks, and buys it with his own money.
Teach older children never to share PINs or OTPs, and never to click links promising free money.
